# Problem 2 - Sakila


```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)
library(microbenchmark)
```


## Load the data

```{r}
if (!dir.exists("./p2/sakila-sqlite3")) {
  if (!dir.exists("p3")) dir.create("p3")
  system(paste(
    "git clone",
    "https://github.com/bradleygrant/sakila-sqlite3.git",
    "./p2/sakila-sqlite3",
    "-q"
  ))
}
```


## Open the database

```{r}
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "./p2/sakila-sqlite3/sakila_master.db")
```


## Part A

For each store, how many customers does that store have, and what percentage of customers of that store are active in the system?

```{r}
a1 <- function() {
  customer_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT store_id, customer_id, active
    FROM customer
  ")
  customer_table |>
    group_by(.data$store_id) |>
    summarise(
      total_customers = n(),
      active_percent = mean(.data$active == 1) * 100
    )
}

a1()
```

```{r}
a2 <- function() {
  dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT 
      store_id,
      COUNT(customer_id) AS total_customers,
      AVG(active) * 100 AS active_percent
    FROM customer
    GROUP BY store_id;
  ")
}

a2()
```

```{r}
microbenchmark(
  a1(),
  a2(),
  times = 100
)
```


Both methods report that there are 2 stores: store 1 has 326 customers, 97.5% are active; while store 2 has 273 customers, 97.4% are active.

The benchmark shows that the second approach is 10x faster than the first one.

## Part B

Generate a table identifying the names and country of each staff member.

```{r}
b1 <- function() {
  staff_table <- dbGetQuery(con,
    "SELECT first_name, last_name, address_id FROM staff"
  )
  address_table <- dbGetQuery(con,
    "SELECT address_id, city_id FROM address"
  )
  city_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT city_id, country_id FROM city")
  country_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT country_id, country FROM country")

  staff_table |>
    inner_join(address_table, by = c("address_id" = "address_id")) |>
    inner_join(city_table, by = c("city_id" = "city_id")) |>
    inner_join(country_table, by = c("country_id" = "country_id")) |>
    select(.data$first_name, .data$last_name, .data$country)
}

b1()
```

```{r}
b2 <- function() {
  dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT first_name, last_name, country
    FROM staff s
      JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
      JOIN city c ON a.city_id = c.city_id
      JOIN country o ON c.country_id = o.country_id
  ")
}

b2()
```

```{r}
microbenchmark(
  b1(),
  b2(),
  times = 100
)
```


Both methods retrieved two staff members. Mike Hillyer from Canada and Jon Stephens from Australia.

This time, the second method is 40x faster than the first one.

## Part C

Identify the name(s) of the film(s) which was/were rented for the highest dollar value.

```{r}
c1 <- function() {
  payment_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT rental_id, amount
    FROM payment
  ")
  rental_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT rental_id, inventory_id
    FROM rental
  ")
  inventory_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT inventory_id, film_id
    FROM inventory
  ")
  film_table <- dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT film_id, title
    FROM film
  ")

  payment_table |>
    inner_join(rental_table, by = c("rental_id" = "rental_id")) |>
    inner_join(inventory_table, by = c("inventory_id" = "inventory_id")) |>
    inner_join(film_table, by = c("film_id" = "film_id")) |>
    group_by(.data$title) |>
    summarise(total_amount = sum(.data$amount)) |>
    arrange(desc(.data$total_amount)) |>
    head(1)
}

c1()
```

```{r}
c2 <- function() {
  dbGetQuery(con, "
    SELECT f.title, sum(amount) total_amount
    FROM payment p
      JOIN rental r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
      JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
      JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    GROUP BY f.film_id
    ORDER BY sum(p.amount) DESC
    LIMIT 1;  
  ")
}

c2()
```

```{r}
microbenchmark(
  c1(),
  c2(),
  times = 100
)
```


Both methods report the film "TELEGRAPH VOYAGE" has highest rented income, which is $231.73.

However, for this case, the first method is slightly faster than the second one.
